opus-5.5.text:
I think it goes back to a kind of dissatisfaction I had early on. When I first started working with data and models, almost everything we did was about correlation: you see patterns, you fit them, you predict the next number. That's useful, but it always felt like we were describing the surface of things without really understanding them. A model could tell you *that* two things move together, but not *why*, and not what would happen if you actually reached in and changed something.

Dynamics and causality, to me, are two sides of the same question: how does the world actually work? Dynamics is about how a system evolves over time, the rules that take you from one state to the next. Causality is about which of those rules are real levers, meaning if you intervene here, what changes there. Once you understand both, you're no longer just observing the world; you can reason about it, imagine counterfactuals, and plan.

There's also a very human side to it. When we think about intelligence, especially in people, so much of it is causal reasoning. A child pushes a cup off the table and learns something about gravity, about cause and effect, from just a few experiences. Our current AI systems often need enormous amounts of data to learn things that humans pick up from a handful of interactions. I suspect a big part of that gap is that we build internal models of dynamics and causes, not just statistical associations.

So for me, studying this isn't just a technical niche. It feels like one of the core questions if we want systems that generalize, that behave sensibly in situations they haven't seen before, and that we can actually trust. And honestly, it's also just intellectually beautiful. There's something deeply satisfying about finding the simple underlying mechanism behind something that looked complicated.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think it goes back to a very simple frustration I had early on: we are incredibly good at describing what is, and surprisingly bad at explaining why it changes. You can take a snapshot of any system, a cell, a market, a model's internal activations, and the snapshot looks clean and legible. But the moment you ask what happens next, or what would have happened if you had intervened, the picture falls apart. That gap is where I've spent most of my attention.

Dynamics is really the study of that "what happens next." Causality is the study of "what if I had done something different." I came to see them as two sides of the same question. A dynamical system tells you how states evolve, but it doesn't by itself tell you which knobs actually matter. Causality gives you the knobs, but without the dynamics you can't tell whether pushing one has an effect that lasts a second or an effect that compounds for years. Most of the interesting problems live right at that intersection.

I'll be honest that part of the interest is also temperamental. I'm uncomfortable with explanations that only work in hindsight. Correlations are cheap, and a story that fits the data after the fact is almost always available. What I want is a model that commits to a prediction before you intervene, and that's a much harder standard. It forces you to be wrong in public, which I think is healthy.

And the reason it feels urgent now is that we're building systems whose behavior we don't fully understand, and then deploying them into other systems we don't fully understand either. If you only have static descriptions, you're flying blind. You need to know how the thing moves and what actually drives it. So for me, dynamics and causality aren't abstract academic interests. They're the minimum toolkit for being responsible about anything that changes over time.
